# Talking head

Someone speaks to camera to tell a story or explain. Speech is the spine
([Cut the speech](../../SKILL.md#cut-the-speech)); this pack covers what goes over
and around it. Voiceover explainers and commentary use the same visual and caption
craft.

Quality bar: complete, fluent, camera-facing sentences; the actual people, documents,
products and events on screen as they are named; a designed opening; emphasis that
follows the meaning. Typical failures: generic stock or drawn filler over a specific
claim, and one caption treatment for the whole video.

## Starting values

Full-height 9:16, usually 1080x1920, upright with no embedded bars. The camera's own
color. Normal speed unless asked; a sped-up edit can keep a normal-speed hook. The
full closing words. The brief and profile decide everything else, including how
densely visuals cover the speech.

## Visuals

- Search for the claim or the named entity, not the topic. An essay opening calls for
  its real title, an endorsement for the actual statement, a policy for the relevant
  passage. Generic AI or server stock rarely explains a specific claim.
- Every named company, school, product, person or place gets its real logo, photo or
  footage on its word. Added animation annotates real imagery (a circle, an arrow, a
  cross-out) or shows what has no real image, such as a feeling or an abstract idea;
  a drawing standing in for something nameable reads as filler and makes the edit
  look simple.
- A comparison shows the actual compared things during that clause, then clears.
  Playful picks keep the literal subject: a robot dog is not a voice recorder. Logos
  beside an aspiration ("we want to raise from…") must not suggest backing.
- Choose evidence when the viewer must inspect a claim, and an illustration or simple
  diagram to explain a process.
- Prefer footage with visible action during its on-screen interval, and check its
  entry and exit; a fade does not replace motion inside the shot. Use a still when the
  evidence exists only as one (a document, a quote, a photo).
- Text cards and image labels standing in for pictures read as filler. Text that is
  part of the source (a headline, a logo, a quoted post) is fine.
- Check spoken numbers before building graphics; tokens, cost, elapsed time and code
  size are different things. If the user keeps an inaccurate sentence, show the
  correction at that sentence and in its caption. Highlight only words present in
  the source.
- Count reuse by original identity: crops and renamed copies are the same visual.
- When no relevant visual exists for a beat, list it for the user instead of filling it.
- Supplied screenshots, tables and demos are evidence: show them whole and long
  enough to read, and shorten a demo by speeding its dead time, not by cutting its result.

## Placement

Choose placement from the shot and the content: a torso-wide card, a lower inset, a
portrait beside the body, a brief full-frame document. Keep faces and important text
readable on a phone. Vary sequence, overlap, scale and position across the video
rather than repeating one layout. Motion directs attention (a restrained entry, a
highlight); blur, extra graphics and transitions need a purpose. For imagery anchored
to a hand, inspect the gesture's start, hold and exit. Captions and visuals are placed
independently.

## Captions

- The opening caption is the hook. Design it as its own composition rather than the
  first subtitle, whether or not a headline was requested; keep it clear of the face
  and hand over to the body captions at a cut. A requested headline uses the user's
  exact words and stays separate from the subtitles. Hooks and headlines follow the
  [text rule](../../SKILL.md#assemble-finish-and-revise): brief, and without a
  background the key word goes on a color box.
- Spread emphasis across the whole dialogue (strong claims, contrasts, numbers,
  payoffs) with quieter phrase captions between them. Pick each
  treatment for what it means: scale, color, placement, a staged reveal, a number
  that counts up, a name in its brand color, deliberate stillness. An accepted design
  is one reference, not the template for the next video.
- Keep captions quiet over dense evidence the viewer must read.
- Body captions are short phrases from the selected speech, clear of faces, visuals
  and platform controls ([caption mechanics](../../references/technical.md#captions)).

## Sound

- Effects mark visible events: a pop as a card appears, a click on an interface
  action, one whoosh on a major scene change. A caption emphasis or a cut can be the
  event. Choose one of two similar variants rather than stacking them.
- Meme sounds (vine boom, bruh, oof) suit deliberately comedic edits; on a sincere
  story they make the moment feel manufactured.
- Land an accent in the gap after its cue word: an effect on a word's onset masks it,
  names worst. Re-transcribing the final mix shows any word an effect covered.
- Clips differ widely in level (`rms_dbfs` in the catalog). Level each effect against
  speech at the same instant ([mixing](../../references/technical.md#voice-loudness-and-mixing));
  peak-matching under-mixes transients.
